title: Computers and Data
sub: Representing text, images and sound with 0 and 1
goal: Explain that all information inside a computer is represented with 0 and 1
Explain, in simple terms, how text, images and sound become numbers

sec.h: Inside a computer, everything is numbers
p: Taking a photo, sending a message, listening to music: inside a computer, all of these are handled as numbers.
And only two digits are used: 0 and 1. Today we will see why 0 and 1 are enough to represent anything.
AI is the same. AI can only calculate with numbers, so turning text and images into numbers is the first step to understanding AI.
A computer contains a huge number of tiny switches that turn electricity on (1) or off (0).
One of these "0 or 1" values is called a bit.
One bit can show 2 patterns. Two bits can show 4, and three bits can show 8. Every extra bit doubles the number of patterns.
Eight bits together make one byte. One byte can show 256 patterns (0 to 255).
The numbers we use every day are decimal. They use ten digits, 0 to 9, and move to the next place at ten.
Binary uses only 0 and 1. Cards make it easy: from the right, line up cards worth 1, 2, 4, 8, 16… each one double the last.
Add up the cards turned to 1, and you get the number. For example, 13 is 8 + 4 + 1, so it is 1101.
Every character has its own number. This is called a character code.
Today we use Unicode, which gives a number to characters from all over the world. The English letter A is number 65, and the Japanese character あ is number 12354.
Nepali, Burmese, Bengali, Sinhala, Chinese, Vietnamese… the characters of your language all have Unicode numbers too. That is why one phone can use many languages.
To save text, a method called UTF-8 turns the numbers into rows of 0s and 1s. An English letter takes 1 byte; most Japanese characters take 3 bytes.

sec.h: There is more than one character encoding: why text gets garbled
p: In the early days of computers, the United States created a character code called ASCII. It represents 128 characters, such as English letters, digits and symbols, with 7 bits.

But 128 characters are not enough for Japanese or Chinese. So countries and regions created their own encodings that use two or more bytes per character (multibyte encodings): Shift_JIS and EUC-JP for Japanese, GBK for Simplified Chinese, Big5 for Traditional Chinese, and others.
Even the same character あ becomes different bytes: 82 A0 in Shift_JIS, A4 A2 in EUC-JP and E3 81 82 in UTF-8.
So if text saved in one encoding is read as another, different characters appear. This is called mojibake (garbled text).
In Myanmar, a system called Zawgyi, separate from Unicode, was widely used for a long time, so the same text could look right on one phone and broken on another.
Unicode was created to end this confusion. Today, almost all web pages in the world use UTF-8.
If you zoom far into an image, you see it is made of tiny squares. These squares are called pixels.
In a black-and-white image, each pixel can be written as 0 or 1, for example white = 0 and black = 1.
In a color image, each pixel's color is made from three kinds of light: red (R), green (G) and blue (B). Each is a number from 0 to 255.
A phone photo is made of millions of these pixels.
Binary uses only 0 and 1, so numbers get very long. That is why hexadecimal is often used. It has 16 symbols: 0–9 and A–F (10–15).
Four binary digits (4 bits) make exactly one hexadecimal digit. So one byte (8 bits) can be written with two hexadecimal digits. Example: 255 = 11111111 = FF.
Color codes on the web, like #FF4F00, write red, green and blue as two hexadecimal digits each: FF = 255, 4F = 79, 00 = 0.
Choose a photo in the tool below to see the color of each pixel in decimal, binary and hexadecimal.
Sound is a vibration of the air: a wave.
We measure the height of this wave again and again at very short intervals and record it as numbers. This is called sampling.
A music CD, for example, measures 44,100 times every second. The more often we measure, the closer we get to the original sound.
AI turns text, images and sound into numbers before it learns.
An AI that recognizes images learns patterns in pixel numbers. An AI that writes text (an LLM) splits text into small pieces called tokens, turns them into numbers, and then calculates.
"Inside a computer, everything is numbers." We will use this idea in every class from now on.

summary: Binary writes numbers as a mix of cards worth 1, 2, 4, 8…
Every character has a number (character codes, Unicode)
There are also country-specific encodings (Shift_JIS, GBK…). Different saved and read encodings cause mojibake
Images are made of pixels; colors are numbers for red, green and blue
One hexadecimal digit = 4 bits. A color code #RRGGBB is red, green and blue in hexadecimal
Sound becomes numbers by measuring the wave many times
AI also turns everything into numbers before it calculates

quiz.q: How many patterns can one bit show?
quiz.e: A bit is either 0 or 1, so it shows 2 patterns.

quiz.q: What is the binary number 1010 in decimal?
What do we call 8 bits together?
quiz.e: 8 bits = 1 byte. One byte can show 256 patterns.

quiz.q: How is the color of a pixel in a color image represented?
o: The strength of red, green and blue
quiz.e: Red (R), green (G) and blue (B) are each a number from 0 to 255.

quiz.q: What does AI do first when it learns from text or images?
quiz.e: AI can only calculate with numbers, so it first turns text and images into numbers.

quiz.q: What happens when text saved in one encoding is read with another?
quiz.e: When the encodings differ, the same bytes are shown as different characters.
